issues.legal_issue: An alienation by a limited owner is supported by legal necessity when serious pressure on the estate exists and the alienee establishes actual necessity or reasonable, bona fide inquiry into the necessity.
material_facts: A limited owner sold part of her inherited property after her husband had died following a prolonged illness, leaving no reliable evidence of property beyond a residence.
She had no other property or income and was responsible for supporting herself and her children, paying rent and municipal taxes, and meeting a daughter’s marriage expenses.
The sale documents recited financial need and debts; the circumstances corroborated pressure on the estate, and one of her sons attested the agreement and sale deed.
issues.conclusion: The alienees amply proved that the sale was supported by legal necessity, and the trial court was right to uphold it.
issues.legal_principle: A limited owner may dispose of the whole estate for legal necessity or benefit to the estate. Legal necessity does not require actual compulsion; it requires pressure on the estate that is serious and sufficient in law. The alienee may discharge the burden by proving actual necessity or proper and bona fide inquiries and reasonable steps to satisfy himself that necessity existed. The Court applied these principles under Hindu law, considering the transferor’s limited ownership under the Dayabhaga system; no earlier cases or statutory provisions are cited.

rule.if: suit_challenges_alienation_for_lack_of_necessity and transferor_is_limited_owner and serious_estate_obligations_exist and circumstances_support_the_stated_need

predicates.suit_challenges_alienation_for_lack_of_n: The proceeding challenges an alienation on the ground that it lacked legal necessity.
predicates.transferor_is_limited_owner: The person who made the alienation held the property as a limited owner.
predicates.serious_estate_obligations_exist: The estate faced obligations or needs that created serious and sufficient pressure on it.
predicates.circumstances_support_the_stated_need: Evidence apart from the stated need, including relevant circumstances, supports the existence of that need.

issues.definition: When a suit challenges an alienation for lack of necessity, the transferor is a limited owner, serious estate obligations exist, and the circumstances support the stated need, the alienation is supported by legal necessity.

issues.legal_issue: Recitals of legal necessity in a deed are admissible but do not alone prove necessity; their weight depends on the circumstances and may increase when the challenger withholds evidence within their special knowledge.
material_facts: The agreement and sale deed recited financial need, debts, and other legal necessity.
The transferor had dependants to support, obligations to pay rent and taxes, marriage expenses to meet, and no other property or income.
The recitals were corroborated by those circumstances, while the plaintiffs’ case that the transfer lacked necessity was not supported by reliable evidence.
issues.conclusion: The recitals were not sufficient by themselves, but they were admissible and, corroborated by the circumstances, supported the finding of legal necessity.
issues.legal_principle: Recitals of legal necessity in a deed do not by themselves prove necessity, but are admissible and may corroborate other evidence. Their weight varies with the circumstances of the transaction. If a challenger withholds evidence within their special knowledge that would normally be unavailable to the alienee, the recitals may carry greater force and an inference may, in an appropriate case, be drawn against the challenger. No earlier cases or statutory provisions are cited.

predicates.suit_challenges_alienation_for_lack_of_n: The proceeding challenges an alienation on the ground that it lacked legal necessity.
predicates.deed_recites_legal_necessity: The deed states that the alienation was made for legal necessity.
predicates.independent_circumstances_corroborate_ne: Evidence apart from the deed’s recital supports the existence of legal necessity.

issues.definition: In a suit challenging an alienation for lack of necessity, a recital of legal necessity is admissible corroborative evidence when independent circumstances support the stated necessity.

issues.legal_issue: A party alleging that consideration recited in a sale deed was not received bears the burden of proving that the recital was false.
material_facts: The sale deed recited payments made at different times, including a payment endorsed before the registering officer.
A witness testified that the transferor received the full consideration.
The plaintiffs alleged that part of the consideration had been taken back, but that allegation was disbelieved, and they made no serious attempt to prove that the remaining amount was unpaid.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs did not prove that the recited consideration was not received, and the Court rejected the finding that the sale was unsupported by full consideration.
issues.legal_principle: The burden lay on the plaintiffs to prove that the consideration recited in the deed was not in fact received and that the recital was false. The Court assessed the deed’s recitals together with the endorsement and witness testimony. No earlier cases or statutory provisions are cited.

predicates.suit_challenges_consideration_recited_in: The proceeding challenges whether consideration stated in a sale deed was paid.
predicates.challenger_alleges_payment_was_not_recei: The party challenging the deed alleges that the transferor did not receive the stated consideration.
predicates.payment_recital_has_supporting_evidence: Evidence such as an endorsement or witness testimony supports the deed’s statement that payment was made.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges payment recited in a sale deed, the challenger alleges nonreceipt, and supporting evidence confirms the payment recital, nonreceipt is not proved.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court cannot sustain a finding of fraud or undue influence on a record containing no supporting evidence when that allegation was not pursued at trial.
material_facts: The plaintiffs pleaded fraud, misrepresentation, and undue influence but no issue was raised and no evidence was led to support that plea.
The trial court recorded that the plea was not seriously pressed because there was no evidence to prove it.
The High Court nevertheless accepted that the transferor had been induced to sell by persuasion and undue influence without addressing that state of the record.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s observations about undue influence and the alleged inducement were unsupported by evidence and seriously vitiated its appreciation of the record.
issues.legal_principle: A finding of fraud or undue influence must be supported by evidence on the record. An appellate court’s conclusion that such conduct occurred cannot stand where the allegation was not pursued and no evidence supports it. No earlier cases or statutory provisions are cited.

predicates.appeal_reviews_validity_of_alienation: The proceeding is an appeal reviewing the validity of an alienation.
predicates.undue_influence_was_not_pursued_at_trial: The party alleging undue influence did not pursue that allegation at trial.
predicates.no_evidence_supports_undue_influence_fin: The record contains no evidence supporting a finding of undue influence.

issues.definition: In an appeal reviewing an alienation, a finding of undue influence cannot be sustained when the allegation was not pursued at trial and the record contains no supporting evidence.

issues.legal_issue: The absence of a deceased defendant’s heirs from an appeal does not defeat the appellants’ claim to dismissal of a suit when the plaintiffs sought no relief against that defendant or those heirs and the relief they sought cannot be granted.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought declaratory relief against the original alienees, asserting that their alienation was not binding, and claimed title to the disputed land.
Although other transferees were joined as parties, the plaintiffs sought no relief against them and pleaded no circumstances explaining their joinder.
The heirs of one such transferee were not brought onto the appellate record; the Court concluded that the plaintiffs’ requested relief against the original alienees could not be granted.
issues.conclusion: The absence of the deceased defendant’s heirs did not affect the appellants’ right to seek dismissal of the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Whether the absence of a deceased party’s heirs affects an appeal depends on the relief claimed. Where the plaintiffs claim relief only against the alienees, claim no relief against the deceased party or successors, and cannot obtain the relief sought against the alienees, the omission of those heirs does not prevent the alienees from seeking dismissal. No earlier cases or statutory provisions are cited.

predicates.appeal_involves_nonjoinder_of_deceased_p: The proceeding is an appeal in which the heirs of a deceased party have not been joined.
predicates.plaintiffs_claim_relief_only_against_ali: The plaintiffs seek relief only against the persons who acquired the property through the alienation.
predicates.relief_against_alienees_cannot_be_grante: The relief sought by the plaintiffs against those alienees cannot be granted.

issues.definition: When an appeal involves the nonjoinder of a deceased party’s heirs, the plaintiffs claim relief only against alienees, and that relief cannot be granted, the nonjoinder does not defeat the alienees’ appeal.
